Why Is the Dyson CameraJet Electric Toothbrush So Expensive?

By Shashank Sharma 5 days ago142 views
  • Share
  • Tweet
0
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 7:34
Instaread

Dyson has spent two decades convincing people to pay premium money for machines that do ordinary jobs extraordinarily well, vacuums, hairdryers, fans, air purifiers. Now it wants to do the same thing to your toothbrush, and the number attached to that ambition is $499.

That is not a typo. The company’s first entry into oral care, the CameraJet, launched on September 1 with a price tag that puts it closer to a mid-range smartphone than anything sitting in a bathroom cup. In India, where the toothbrush hasn’t officially launched yet, the same math works out to roughly Rs 47,000 once you convert the US price, well before any import duty gets added on top.

So what exactly are you paying for, and does any of it hold up once the novelty wears off?

What the CameraJet Actually Is

Strip away the marketing language and the CameraJet is three devices stitched into one handle: an electric toothbrush, a water flosser, and a tiny camera system that watches your mouth while you brush.

The camera is the part doing all the talking. Dyson has built in a 100,000-pixel macro lens that captures 28 images every second from inside your mouth. Those images feed into a machine-learning system Dyson calls Gap Optical Targeting, which is trained to spot the narrow gaps between teeth where plaque tends to build up and a regular brush head simply cannot reach.

When the system identifies one of those gaps, it doesn’t just flag it, it acts on it. A built-in jet fires a targeted burst of mouthrinse straight into the gap within about 100 milliseconds of detection, effectively flossing that spot while the bristles are still working the surface. Dyson is calling this “flossing while you brush,” and on paper it solves a real problem: most people brush daily but skip flossing more often than they’d admit to their dentist.

The mouthrinse itself lives in a 12.5ml reservoir inside the handle, refilled in about three seconds by the charging dock. Dyson has also engineered what it calls an “anti-gravity tank” a diaphragm pump and pressure chamber designed to keep the rinse flowing evenly even when the brush is tilted or held horizontally to reach your back teeth, which is normally where water flossers with simple straw-fed reservoirs tend to struggle.

Pair the toothbrush with the MyDyson app and you get a live video feed from inside your own mouth, along with coverage mapping and pressure alerts if you’re brushing too hard. Dyson has been upfront about the obvious privacy question here — the camera only activates during live viewing or automatic jetting, none of the footage is recorded or stored on the device, and nothing gets uploaded to the cloud, according to the company.

Where the $499 Actually Goes

A price this far above category norms usually means one of two things: aggressive brand-tax pricing, or genuine engineering cost that has to be recovered somewhere. Dyson’s numbers point more toward the second, even if the final retail price still leaves plenty of room for margin.

The company says CameraJet took six years and 661 engineers to build, and that the Gap Optical Targeting model was trained on more than 470,000 dental images before it could reliably tell a food particle from a gap between teeth in real time, underwater, through toothpaste foam and saliva. The finished device runs on roughly 16 million lines of code, a figure that would sound absurd for a toothbrush if you didn’t already know it came with a live camera feed and a real-time AI vision model running inside a bathroom appliance the size of a pen.

Compare that to what a premium electric toothbrush from Oral-B or Philips Sonicare actually is under the hood: a motor, a pressure sensor, a battery, and a Bluetooth chip talking to an app that mostly just counts your brushing time. Those brushes typically sit in the $150–$300 range and have done so for years, because the hardware inside them hasn’t fundamentally changed. CameraJet is a different category of product wearing a toothbrush’s shape, and Dyson is pricing it like one.

That said, price and value are not the same conversation, and it’s fair to ask whether an at-home camera and an AI flossing jet solve a problem worth $499, when floss costs about three dollars a roll.

Is It Actually Worth It?

The honest answer is: it depends entirely on why you’d buy one.

If you’re the kind of person who genuinely struggles to floss consistently and dental surveys have consistently shown most adults fall into that bucket. CameraJet is solving a real behavioral problem, not a fake one. Automating the one dental-hygiene step people skip most often has legitimate value, and being able to actually watch the gaps in your own teeth in real time is the kind of feedback loop that tends to change habits faster than a dentist telling you to floss more at your six-month checkup.

If you’re comparing it purely as a toothbrush, though, $499 buys a lot of brushing technique correction from any $30 electric toothbrush with a pressure sensor. The core brushing mechanism in CameraJet three intensity modes, oscillation, pressure alerts isn’t meaningfully different from what Oral-B and Philips have offered for years at a fraction of the cost. You’re not paying for better brushing. You’re paying for the camera, the AI, and the six years of R&D that went into making that camera small enough to fit in a toothbrush head without blinding you with reflected light off your own enamel.

There’s also the practical matter of maintenance cost that doesn’t show up in the headline price replacement brush heads, mouthrinse refills if you don’t use tap water, and the fact that this is a first-generation Dyson product in a category the company has never shipped in before. Dyson’s vacuums and hair tools earned their premium pricing over multiple product generations. CameraJet is asking for that same premium on day one.

Where You Can Actually Buy One

CameraJet went on sale September 2 in the US at $499.99, and in the UK at £419.99, available in Ceramic Pink and Ceramic Ultra Blue. The full Dyson Dental System bundle, toothbrush, charging dock, travel case, toothpaste, and mouthrinse, comes at a premium over the standalone device price depending on the market.

India doesn’t have a confirmed release date yet. Dyson’s India website currently only allows you to register for availability updates, and the company has said local pricing and launch timing will be announced closer to the actual release. Given Dyson’s established retail presence in India through its own stores and marketplace listings, a launch is likely, but anyone quoting an exact India price right now is estimating off the US number rather than repeating anything Dyson has confirmed.

The Bottom Line

Dyson didn’t build CameraJet because the toothbrush market was crying out for a $500 option, it built it because a camera-and-AI system that can floss for you while you brush is a genuinely hard engineering problem, and Dyson’s whole business model is charging a premium for solving hard engineering problems most people didn’t ask anyone to solve. Whether that’s worth it to you comes down to a simpler question than the spec sheet suggests: do you need a reason to finally floss, or do you just need a better toothbrush? CameraJet is built, and priced, for the first person. Everyone else can keep the $3 roll of floss.
